stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Archaeologists often radiocarbon date ancient hearths by testing the charcoal left inside them. Archaeologist Ilse Moravec points out, however, that a log from a tree that lived for centuries may contain carbon absorbed long before the wood was ever burned, so its charcoal can yield an age far older than the fire itself. When Moravec's team excavated hearths at a highland site, they set the abundant charcoal aside and submitted only charred seeds of wild annual grasses for dating. This choice suggests that in Moravec's view, ______
choices: charcoal from long-lived trees gives more accurate hearth dates than charred annual seeds do.
charred seeds from annual plants better indicate when the hearths were in use than charcoal does.
radiocarbon dating cannot produce a trustworthy age for any material recovered from a hearth.
the people who built the hearths deliberately cultivated annual grasses close to the site.
explanation: Ask why Moravec would set aside plentiful charcoal and date only seeds. She has explained that old wood can make charcoal look older than the fire. A plant that lives for a single year can't carry centuries-old carbon. Her choice only makes sense if she thinks the seeds track the time of the fire more closely than the charcoal does.

A.why: You reversed the comparison. Moravec put the charcoal aside because she distrusts it. She would not do that if she thought it gave the better date.

C.why: You went too far. Moravec still used radiocarbon dating, just on different material. She thinks one material is flawed, not the method as a whole.

D.why: You credited Moravec with a belief her action doesn't need. The grasses are described as wild, and she chose them for how long they live, not for how people used them.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: For decades, the standard way to census reef fish has been the diver transect: a scuba diver swims a fixed line and records every fish seen. Marine biologist Teodora Quispe has noted that groupers and several other wary species tend to retreat into crevices as a diver approaches, while bolder species such as damselfish appear unaffected. Quispe now recommends supplementing transects with cameras mounted on the reef and left unattended for several hours. Quispe's recommendation implies that she believes ______
choices: diver transects produce counts too unreliable to be useful for any reef species at all.
unattended cameras tend to record fewer groupers on a reef than diver transects do.
damselfish populations have been overestimated in most past censuses of reef fish.
diver transects likely record fewer wary fish than are actually present on a reef.
explanation: The flaw Quispe names is that wary fish hide when a diver comes near. Cameras left alone remove the diver. She recommends them because she thinks transects miss some of the wary fish that are really there.

A.why: You went too far. Quispe wants to supplement transects, not replace them, and she says bold species seem unaffected. She thinks transects are limited, not useless.

B.why: You reversed the comparison. The cameras are meant to catch the groupers that hide from divers. Quispe would expect them to record more groupers, not fewer.

C.why: You invented a problem the passage never raises. Damselfish appear unaffected by divers, so nothing suggests they have been miscounted, let alone overcounted.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Forecasts of overnight fog in one river valley in northern Spain have traditionally relied on ground-level weather stations, which measure temperature and humidity about two meters above the surface. After several fog events went unpredicted, meteorologist Rafael Ochoa arranged for tethered balloons to record temperature at intervals up to 300 meters above the valley floor each evening. Ochoa's decision suggests that he suspected ______
choices: conditions above the height of the ground stations influence whether fog forms in the valley.
the ground stations had been recording humidity incorrectly on evenings when fog formed.
fog in the valley forms first at about 300 meters and then sinks toward the valley floor.
readings taken near the surface explain valley fog better than readings taken higher up.
explanation: Ochoa's response to the missed forecasts was to measure the air above the stations' two-meter height. That only makes sense if he thought something happening higher up affects fog and the ground readings were missing it.

B.why: This is the extra-step trap. Ochoa didn't repair or replace the ground instruments. He added measurements at other heights. His action shows he thought the stations were incomplete, not that they were wrong.

C.why: You read a specific theory into the 300-meter figure. That is just the top of the measurement range. Nothing shows Ochoa expected fog to start there.

D.why: You reversed the comparison. Ochoa added higher readings because the surface readings had failed. He would not do that if he thought the surface readings were enough.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Manufacturers usually rate a new polymer adhesive by its strength immediately after curing. Materials scientist Hana Okafor has found, however, that while some adhesives keep nearly all their strength after months of humid exposure, others lose more than half, even when their initial strengths were identical. When selecting a sealant for bridge cables, Okafor's lab evaluated candidates only after storing samples for six months at 90 percent humidity. This testing approach suggests that Okafor thinks ______
choices: the adhesives that are strongest right after curing tend to weaken the most in humid conditions.
an adhesive's strength after humid storage is best predicted by its strength right after curing.
strength right after curing is an unreliable guide to how an adhesive will perform when damp.
humidity weakens every polymer adhesive by roughly half within the first six months of use.
explanation: Look at the split result. Adhesives that started equally strong ended up very different after humid exposure, so the starting number didn't predict what happened later. Okafor tested only after long humid storage, which shows she doesn't trust the standard after-curing rating to tell her how a sealant will hold up when damp.

A.why: You invented a pattern. Okafor's finding concerns adhesives with identical starting strength. It doesn't say stronger adhesives weaken more. Her result points to no link, not a reversed one.

B.why: You reversed her conclusion. Equal starting strengths led to very different outcomes, which is exactly why she stopped relying on the after-curing measurement.

D.why: Check the 'while' clause. Some adhesives kept nearly all their strength, so humidity does not weaken every adhesive by half.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Many conservation groups judge the success of a wetland restoration by counting the plant species that return to it. Ecologist Maren Solberg argues, however, that a restored marsh can host dozens of plant species while still failing to remove nitrogen from farm runoff as effectively as a natural marsh does. In monitoring a restored marsh in Denmark, Solberg's team sampled the water entering and leaving the site in addition to surveying its vegetation. This approach suggests that Solberg believes ______
choices: plant species counts are irrelevant to judging any aspect of a restored wetland's condition.
restored marshes with more plant species remove less nitrogen than those with fewer species.
water sampling reveals less about a restoration's success than a survey of vegetation does.
plant species counts alone cannot show whether a restored marsh filters runoff as intended.
explanation: Solberg says a marsh can be rich in plant species and still filter poorly. So she adds water sampling, which measures filtering directly. Her method depends on the belief that species counts by themselves leave that question open.

A.why: You went too far. Solberg's team still surveyed the vegetation. She thinks species counts are not enough on their own, not that they don't matter.

B.why: This is strength creep into a pattern she never claimed. She says species-rich marshes can still filter poorly, not that more species means less filtering.

C.why: You reversed the comparison. Solberg added water sampling because vegetation surveys miss something. She would not see it as the less informative measure.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Folktale collections assembled in the nineteenth century typically printed a single authoritative version of each tale, often edited together from several tellings. Folklorist Amaru Condori contends that such editing erased the variations that reveal how storytellers adapted tales for particular audiences. In compiling a new archive of Andean trickster stories, Condori recorded every telling separately, noting the narrator, the setting, and who was listening. Condori's method suggests that he regards ______
choices: nineteenth-century collections as containing no authentic material about any of their tales.
the differences between individual tellings of a tale as worth preserving for later study.
a single edited version as more revealing about storytellers than separate recordings are.
Andean trickster stories as having changed more over time than other folktales have.
explanation: Condori criticizes editing because it removes the differences between tellings. He records each telling separately and notes who was listening. That approach only makes sense if he thinks those differences are valuable evidence worth keeping.

A.why: You went too far. Condori objects to how the old collections merged tellings. He never says their contents are inauthentic.

C.why: You reversed the comparison. Condori says edited versions hide how storytellers adapted tales. That is why he records tellings separately.

D.why: You credited Condori with a belief his method doesn't need. He applies it to Andean stories but makes no comparison with other traditions.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Hospitals in many regions track influenza activity by counting patients who test positive for the virus. Epidemiologist Sunita Rao notes, though, that many people with mild flu never seek care, so hospital counts mainly reflect severe cases and can lag behind community spread by a week or more. On Rao's advice, a regional health department has begun testing wastewater from treatment plants twice weekly for influenza genetic material. The department's decision suggests that in its view, ______
choices: hospital test counts alone give an incomplete and often delayed picture of community flu.
hospital test counts should no longer be used to monitor influenza within the region.
people with mild flu are more likely than severe cases to appear in hospital test data.
influenza now spreads through the region more quickly than it did in earlier seasons.
explanation: Rao describes two flaws in hospital counts: they miss mild cases and they lag behind community spread. The department added wastewater testing on her advice. That only makes sense if it agrees hospital counts alone leave gaps.

B.why: You went too far. The department began wastewater testing, but nothing says it stopped using hospital counts. It thinks they are limited, not worthless.

C.why: You reversed the comparison. The passage says mild cases often never reach hospitals, so hospital data mainly reflects severe cases.

D.why: You credited the department with a belief it never needed. Its decision answers a weakness in how flu is measured. It doesn't depend on any change in how fast flu spreads.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Engineers have long inspected steel highway bridges by eye, looking for cracks and rust during scheduled visits every two years. Structural engineer Kofi Mensah observes that fatigue cracks often begin inside welded joints, where they remain invisible from the surface until they have grown large. For a newly built river crossing, Mensah specified ultrasonic sensors embedded at each major weld, transmitting readings continuously to the transportation agency. Mensah's specification implies that he believes ______
choices: visual inspections have never identified a fatigue crack in any steel highway bridge.
welded joints are a less likely site of fatigue cracking than exposed steel surfaces.
visual inspections can fail to detect fatigue cracks while those cracks are still small.
bridges over rivers develop fatigue cracks faster than bridges built over dry land.
explanation: The flaw Mensah names is that cracks inside welds can't be seen until they are large. Sensors placed at the welds address exactly that. Specifying them shows he thinks visual inspection can miss cracks at an early stage.

A.why: This is strength creep. Mensah says internal cracks stay invisible until they grow large, which means inspectors can see them once they are large. He thinks visual checks are late, not that they never work.

B.why: You reversed the claim. Mensah says fatigue cracks often begin in welded joints, which is why he put the sensors there.

D.why: You fixed on an incidental detail. The bridge happens to cross a river, but Mensah's reasoning is about welds and what inspectors can see. Where the bridge sits plays no part.
